section.title: Principles of Marriage
section.sectionRationale: Having addressed sexual immorality, Paul turns to the questions the Corinthians wrote about marriage, singleness, and sexual duty. Against both those who prized abstinence even within marriage and those who excused immorality, he teaches mutual self-giving in marriage, honors singleness and marriage each as a gift, forbids divorce, shows how a believing spouse sanctifies the home, and grounds it all in the principle of remaining faithfully in the calling in which God has placed you, because you were bought at a price.
section.thesis: Marriage is a good gift in which husband and wife belong to one another in mutual self-giving, singleness is likewise a gift, divorce is forbidden and the believing spouse sanctifies the home, and above all each believer, bought at a price, should live out their faith in the situation to which God has called them.
section.frameNote: Four movements: mutual duty and self-giving in marriage; directions to the unmarried, widows, and married against divorce; the mixed marriage and the sanctifying believer; and the governing rule, remain in your calling, for you were bought at a price.

verses.text: Now for the matters you wrote about: It is good to abstain from sexual relations.
But because there is so much {{porneia|sexual immorality}}, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband.
The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband.
The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife.

Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control.
I say this as a concession, not as a command.
I wish that all men were as I am. But each man has his own {{charisma|gift}} from God; one has this gift, another has that.
Now to the unmarried and widows I say this: It is good for them to remain unmarried, as I am.
But if they cannot control themselves, let them marry. For it is better to marry than to burn with passion.
To the married I give this command (not I, but the Lord): A wife must not {{chorizo|separate}} from her husband.
But if she does, she must remain unmarried or else be reconciled to her husband. And a husband must not divorce his wife.
To the rest I say this (I, not the Lord): If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her.
And if a woman has an unbelieving husband and he is willing to live with her, she must not divorce him.

For the unbelieving husband is {{hagiazo|sanctified}} through his believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is sanctified through her believing husband. Otherwise your children would be unclean, but now they are holy.
But if the unbeliever leaves, let him go. The believing brother or sister is not bound in such cases. God has called you to live in peace.
How do you know, wife, whether you will save your husband? Or how do you know, husband, whether you will save your wife?
Regardless, each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned to him and to which God has called him. This is what I prescribe in all the churches.
Was a man already circumcised when he was called? He should not become uncircumcised. Was a man still uncircumcised when called? He should not be circumcised.
Circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing. Keeping God’s commandments is what counts.
Each one should remain in the situation he was in when he was {{kaleo|called}}.
Were you a slave when you were called? Do not let it concern you; but if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.
For he who was a slave when he was called by the Lord is the Lord’s freedman. Conversely, he who was a free man when he was called is Christ’s slave.
You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men.
Brothers, each one should remain in the situation he was in when God called him.

porneia.gloss: Sexual immorality of every kind. In a city saturated with it, Paul commends marriage as the God-given context for sexual life, not as a mere remedy but as the honorable and normal setting in which desire is rightly expressed within faithful covenant love.

charisma.gloss: A gift of grace, something freely given by God. Paul calls both singleness and marriage a charisma, a grace fitted to each person. Neither state is second class; each is a gift from God to be received and used for His service.

chorizo.gloss: To separate, to part, to divide. Paul relays the Lord's own command that a wife must not separate from her husband. The word underlines the permanence of the marriage bond and the seriousness of tearing apart what God has joined.

hagiazo.gloss: To sanctify, to set apart as holy. The unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the believing partner, and the children are holy. This is not automatic salvation but a covenantal setting apart: the believing spouse brings the household into the sphere of God's grace and gospel witness.

kaleo.gloss: To call, to summon. God's effective call to salvation reaches people in every station of life. Paul's repeated point is that the call does not require changing one's outward situation; the believer is to live faithfully for Christ right where the call found them.

basic.context: The Corinthians had written to Paul with questions about sex, marriage, and singleness. Some thought the holiest thing was to avoid sex altogether, even in marriage. Paul answers with balance: within marriage, husband and wife owe themselves to each other; singleness and marriage are both gifts from God; married couples must not divorce; and where one spouse believes and the other does not, the believer should stay and let the gospel work. The thread running through it all is to remain faithfully with God in the life you were called in, because you were bought at a price.
basic.hermeneutics: Paul distinguishes the Lord's direct command, do not divorce, from his own Spirit-led counsel for new situations the Gospels did not directly address, such as mixed marriages. He is not lowering the authority of his teaching but showing which words trace directly to Jesus. The section is pastoral wisdom, applying gospel principles to real questions.
basic.originalLanguages: Marriage guards against porneia, sexual immorality, by giving desire its rightful home. Both singleness and marriage are a charisma, a gift of grace from God. The Lord forbids a wife to chorizo, to separate, from her husband. A believing spouse can hagiazo, sanctify, set apart, the unbelieving partner and children. And the governing idea is kaleo, God's call, which reaches us in every station and asks us to remain faithfully there.
basic.typology: Marriage itself points beyond itself: the one flesh union of husband and wife is a shadow of Christ and His church. The sanctifying of a household through one believer echoes how holiness spreads from the covenant head to those under him, fulfilled in Christ who sanctifies His people.
basic.christ: The command against divorce is the Lord's own, showing Jesus as the authority over marriage. The deepest ground of the chapter is that we were bought at a price: Christ's purchase makes every believer, slave or free, married or single, the Lord's freedman and Christ's slave, belonging first and finally to Him.
basic.god: God is the giver of every good gift, including both marriage and singleness. He calls people to Himself in every walk of life, and He is a God of peace, not compulsion. He works even through a believing spouse to set apart a home for grace.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 2 gives the one flesh union that underlies Paul's teaching. Malachi 2 records God's hatred of divorce and His purpose for faithful marriage. Mark 10 preserves Jesus' own command that no one separate what God joined. Ephesians 5 shows marriage as a picture of Christ and the church.
basic.oneStory: From the first marriage in the garden to the marriage of the Lamb, Scripture treats the union of husband and wife as good and as a sign of God's covenant love. Paul applies that story to Corinth: honor marriage, honor singleness, keep faith with your spouse, and above all keep faith with the Lord who bought you, wherever He has called you.

context.literary:
Chapter 7 opens a new section of the letter. Up to now Paul has answered what he has heard from Chloe's people, 1:11, and from general report, 5:1. From 7:1 he turns to what the Corinthians wrote, and the marker is 'Now for the matters you wrote about,' which comes back as 'now about' at 7:25, 8:1, 12:1, 16:1 and 16:12. Each time a new subject begins.

The chapter is a series of paired instructions. Verses 2 to 5 give a perfect mirror: husband and wife are addressed in turn, 'likewise' links every clause, and the same weight falls on each. In the Greek world and the Jewish one, instructions about marriage were usually addressed to men. Here every duty is stated twice, once for each partner. The same pairing shows up in verses 10 to 14, where the wife is named before the husband in the command about divorce, and the believing husband and the believing wife are given parallel directions.

The passage also keeps changing the source of authority. Verse 6 is 'a concession, not a command.' Verse 10 is 'not I, but the Lord.' Verse 12 is 'I, not the Lord.' Verse 25, later in the chapter, will add 'I have no command from the Lord.' These labels are not signs of doubt but of honesty about what comes straight from the teaching of Jesus and what Paul gives as a trustworthy apostle applying it to new cases.

Verses 17 to 24 widen the lens. Paul draws a general rule, 'each one should lead the life that the Lord has assigned,' and then illustrates it twice, circumcision and slavery, before repeating the rule in verse 24. The rule is stated at the start and the end of the illustrations, and the verb 'called' and its noun recur again and again in verses 15 to 24, so the whole unit is a meditation on the word.
context.historical:
Roman law and custom shaped what the Corinthians would have heard. Augustus had passed laws to promote marriage and childbearing, and penalised the unmarried and childless in matters of inheritance, so a gospel that honoured singleness cut across the official mood. Divorce was also easy in Roman society. Either partner could end a marriage by simple declaration, without a court, and the wife could initiate it. That is likely why Paul addresses both husband and wife in verses 10 and 11, whereas Jewish custom normally gave the right of divorce to the man. Mark 10:11-12 shows Jesus' teaching applied to both sexes in the same way.

In the Greek world there was also a strand of thought that treated sexual relations as a lower activity. Some in Corinth may have claimed that the spiritual person should abstain, even within marriage, and 7:1 probably reflects that: 'It is good to abstain from sexual relations' is Paul quoting or answering a line from their letter. The footnote in the BSB gives the Greek literally, 'It is good for a man not to touch a woman.' Against that background, Paul's careful insistence in verses 3 to 5 that married people owe each other sexual relations was radical.

The mixed marriages of verses 12 to 16 were common in a young church. Women converts, especially, were sometimes married to men who followed other gods. In the Greek household, the husband's religion was normally the household's religion, so a wife who changed faith risked a serious clash.

Slavery was part of the fabric of Corinth, and the church included slaves and the free. A slave had no legal control over his body, marriage or work. A freedman, as Paul's 'freedman of the Lord' recalls, remained bound by duties to his former master. Circumcision, meanwhile, was a living question where Jews and Gentiles met in the church, and Paul's answer here anticipates the one he gives in Galatians.
context.canonical:
Paul's teaching rests on creation. Genesis 2:18-24 says that it is not good for the man to be alone and describes the one flesh union. Jesus drew on the same verses when asked about divorce, Mark 10:6-9 and Matthew 19:3-9, and Paul's 'not I, but the Lord' in verse 10 is a pointer to that teaching. The command that what God has joined, man must not separate, stands behind verses 10 and 11.

The idea that spouses owe each other is not new in Scripture. Exodus 21:10 required a husband not to reduce the food, clothing or marital rights of his wife, so marital rights were already treated as something a person was owed. Song of Songs 6:3, 'I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me,' states the mutual belonging that Paul describes in verse 4.

The prohibition of divorce for a believer with an unbelieving partner stands in contrast to Ezra 10:3, where the returned exiles covenanted to send away foreign wives, and Paul takes the opposite path. Peter later gives practical advice about the same situation, 1 Peter 3:1-2: wives who are married to unbelievers may win them 'without words' by their behaviour. Household faith is also seen in Acts 16:31-34, where the jailer and his household are baptised.

The call to remain where you were called anticipates Galatians 3:28 and 5:6, where status in Christ outweighs status in the world, and it stands beside Ephesians 6:5-9 and Philemon 15-16, where slaves and masters are told how to live as brothers. The closing words, 'You were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men,' repeat 6:20 and recall Leviticus 25:42, 'they are not to be sold as slaves.' Finally, Ephesians 5:22-33 gives the fullest New Testament picture of marriage, as a sign of Christ and the church.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul writes to correct two errors at once. One group in Corinth thought that the spiritual life required abstinence, even within marriage. The other treated the body as unimportant and excused immorality. He steers between them by treating marriage as a place of generous mutual giving and by treating celibacy as a real gift, not a rank. The test of both is whether each person is serving the Lord in the way he or she has been given.

He also wants the Corinthians to take the permanence of marriage seriously. By quoting the Lord's own command against divorce, he makes clear that the question is not one for private preference. But he is equally careful to show where he is making a judgment about situations Jesus did not directly address, such as a believer married to an unbeliever, so that no one confuses his counsel with the Lord's command.

The last section is the key to the whole. Whether married or unmarried, circumcised or not, slave or free, each believer has been called and bought. Paul wants them to stop treating their circumstances as the main thing, and start treating their relationship with the Lord who assigned them as the main thing. His readers are not to rush out of their situation to find a more spiritual one, but to find the Lord within the one they have.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Paul labels his statements, and the labels tell us how to apply them. 'I say this as a concession, not as a command,' verse 6, tells us that the temporary abstention of verse 5 is permitted, not required. 'Not I, but the Lord,' verse 10, tells us that the prohibition of divorce is an abiding command. 'I, not the Lord,' verse 12, signals apostolic counsel, which does not carry less authority but addresses a case Jesus did not discuss, and Paul says in verse 40 that he has the Spirit of God.

The description of the Corinthian situation should not be turned into a general rule. Verse 26 and the discussion of 'remain as you are' in verses 17 to 24 are written to people facing particular pressures. Reading verse 17 as a command never to change job, marry or leave a bad situation would conflict with verse 21, where a slave is told to gain freedom if he can. The principle is contentment and faithfulness within God's call, not a ban on change.

Some sentences describe and do not endorse. Verse 5 acknowledges that Satan may tempt through lack of self-control. It does not make sexual relations a mere remedy for lust. Verse 9, 'better to marry than to burn,' reads like a remedy, but verses 2 to 4 have already set marriage in a larger setting of mutual love and duty. The prescription is to honour one's marriage and singleness alike as gifts.

debates.question: Is 'It is good to abstain from sexual relations' in verse 1 Paul's own view, or a Corinthian slogan he answers?

views.label: A slogan quoted from their letter
views.case: Paul begins 'Now for the matters you wrote about,' and the line reads like a claim from the letter. Verses 2 to 5 then qualify it sharply: because of immorality, each should have a spouse, and married people owe each other. On this reading Paul grants part of the claim and refuses the rest, a pattern he follows with the slogans of 6:12-13. Many modern translators use quotation marks for this reason, and the BSB footnote gives the literal Greek, 'not to touch a woman.'

views.label: Paul's own preference, then qualified
views.case: Others hear Paul stating his own view, supported by verses 7 and 8, where he wishes that all were as he is and says it is good for the unmarried and widows to remain so. In that case verse 1 is a statement that singleness is good, followed by the recognition that most people need marriage.

debates.bearing: Either way Paul does not allow the claim to cancel marriage. The consequence for the church is that sexual abstention inside marriage is never the higher path, and singleness is a gift for those who have it, not a standard for all.

debates.question: Does 'make use of it' in verse 21 mean gaining freedom or staying a slave?

views.label: Take the opportunity to be free
views.case: The BSB reads 'if you can gain your freedom, take the opportunity.' The Greek has only 'rather use,' with nothing said about what is used. Many commentators take it to mean use the opportunity of freedom, because Paul speaks of gaining freedom immediately beforehand and because he tells them not to become slaves of men in verse 23.

views.label: Rather make use of your slavery
views.case: Others supply 'slavery' as the thing to be used. Paul has just said that it should not trouble the slave, and the whole section is about staying in one's calling. On this reading he means: even if you can be free, make the most of being a slave for the Lord. Most scholars find it hard to square with verse 23, but the grammar permits it.

debates.bearing: Paul does not endorse slavery in either case. He wants slaves to know that their dignity does not depend on their legal status, he welcomes freedom when it is offered, and he tells all believers never to treat themselves as owned by men.

debates.question: Does Paul permit remarriage after a marriage breaks down?

views.label: Remarriage restricted
views.case: Verse 11 tells the separated wife to remain unmarried or be reconciled, suggesting the bond endures and remarriage is not freely open while the spouse lives.

views.label: The abandoned believer is not bound
views.case: Verse 15 says the believer deserted by an unbeliever is not bound, which many read as freedom from the marriage, and thus in some cases freedom to remarry in the Lord.

debates.bearing: All orthodox readings uphold the permanence of marriage and forbid casual divorce; they differ on how far verse 15 releases an abandoned believer, and pastoral care must weigh both texts with compassion and holiness.

debates.question: What does it mean that the unbelieving spouse and children are sanctified?

views.label: Covenantal setting apart, not automatic salvation
views.case: The household is brought within the sphere of grace and gospel witness through the believer, but each person still needs personal faith, as verse 16 shows by asking whether the spouse will be saved.

views.label: A ground for hope and continued marriage
views.case: The holiness of the home is Paul's reason not to divorce; the believer's presence is a means God may use toward the salvation of the family.

debates.bearing: Both readings deny that sanctified here means already saved; it assures the believer that the marriage and children are not defiled but set within reach of God's saving grace.

study.originalLanguages:
Paul's choice of words in verses 3 to 5 shows his care. The 'marital duty' of verse 3 is literally the 'debt,' opheile, that is to be paid, and the verb is the one used for giving back what is owed. The word suggests that each partner owes something to the other, and that giving it is not a favour but an act of justice and love. Verse 4 states the basis: neither has 'authority,' exousiazo, over his own body. It is the same verb Paul used in 6:12, 'I will not be mastered,' and the effect is to say that in marriage neither partner is ruled by the self and both are ruled by the other.

In verse 5, 'do not deprive,' is apostereo, the same verb as 'cheat' in 6:7-8. Withholding what is owed in marriage is a form of defrauding. The exception, 'by mutual consent,' translates symphonos, from which the English 'symphony' comes, and the permitted reason, to 'devote yourselves to prayer,' uses scholazo, to have leisure for something. The pause is meant to be an act of freedom with a purpose, not a withdrawal. 'Lack of self-control' is akrasia, the opposite of the enkrateia Paul asks for in verse 9.

The word for a 'concession' in verse 6 is sungnome, a permission granted in view of weakness. Verse 9's 'burn' is the passive of puroo, 'to be set on fire,' used of passion that cannot be managed.

The two verbs for ending a marriage are different. In verses 10 and 11 the wife is told not to 'separate,' chorizo, and the husband not to 'divorce,' aphiemi, literally 'send away.' Verse 15 returns to chorizo for the unbeliever who leaves. Then Paul says the believer 'is not bound,' ou dedoulotai, literally 'has not been enslaved.' The verb is douloo, not the deo of 7:27 and 7:39, 'bound' to a spouse. That difference is much discussed, since it suggests that the abandoned believer is no longer under the same obligation, though how far it reaches is debated.

In verse 14, the children are 'unclean,' akatharta, but now 'holy,' hagia. These are the vocabulary of the Old Testament, where clean and holy marked the camp of Israel, and Paul reverses the normal flow: holiness flows from believer to household, not contamination in the other direction.

The repeated 'called' in verses 15 to 24, kaleo and the noun klesis, becomes a technical term for the place in life where one meets God's summons. Verse 17's 'prescribe' translates diatasso, which Paul uses for apostolic rulings given to all the churches, 11:34 and 16:1. Verse 22 contrasts the 'freedman,' apeleutheros, with the 'slave,' doulos, and in Roman life a freedman still owed duties to his patron, so 'freedman of the Lord' means freed but still belonging to Him.

typology.fulfillment: The union of man and woman in Eden is the pattern behind Paul's insistence that husband and wife belong to each other, verse 4. Paul later says that this union is a mystery that points to Christ and the church, Ephesians 5:31-32. The escalation is from a union of two persons to a union between the Son of God and a redeemed people, in which He gives Himself up for her, Ephesians 5:25. The type falls short because human marriage can be broken by death and failure, Romans 7:2, whereas the bond of Christ with His church cannot, and Revelation 19:7-9 shows its wedding day.

typology.type: Household holiness at the Passover, Exodus 12:3
typology.fulfillment: The Passover was kept by households, each with its own lamb, and the household was marked and spared by the blood. The same sense of a household brought under God's care runs through verse 14, where an unbelieving partner and children are 'sanctified' through a believer. The pattern comes to fulfilment in the promise of Acts 16:31, 'you and your household,' and in the household baptisms of Acts 16:33. The type is incomplete in that the Passover protected a household physically, while the gospel calls each person to personal faith, as verse 16 reminds the reader.

typology.type: Freed people who belong to their God, Leviticus 25:42
typology.fulfillment: Israel was told that they were not to be sold as slaves because they were God's servants whom He had brought out of Egypt. Paul's 'you were bought at a price; do not become slaves of men' is that principle at a higher level. The Lord's freedman and Christ's slave, verse 22, belongs first to Him. The correspondence deepens because the price is the blood of Christ, 1 Peter 1:18-19, and because the ownership extends to every believer, not only the people of one nation. The type falls short in that the exodus was a rescue from a single empire, while the redemption in Christ rescues from sin and death.

typology.type: The sign of the covenant, Genesis 17:10-11
typology.fulfillment: Circumcision marked Abraham's family as belonging to God. Paul declares that 'circumcision is nothing and uncircumcision is nothing,' and that what counts is keeping God's commandments, verse 19. The sign points beyond itself to a heart marked by God, Deuteronomy 30:6, and Paul later says that in Christ believers were circumcised 'with a circumcision not performed by human hands,' Colossians 2:11. The type is fulfilled when the sign is replaced by the reality, and it falls short in that a physical mark could be given without the heart that it signified.

study.christ:
The chapter points to Christ first by authority. In verse 10 Paul says 'not I, but the Lord,' and he is referring to the teaching Jesus gave in the Gospels. Jesus took the question of divorce back to creation, 'from the beginning of creation, God made them male and female,' Mark 10:6, and said that what God has joined together, man must not separate, Mark 10:9. When Paul has that word, he hands it on without softening it. When he has not, he says so, 'I, not the Lord,' verse 12, and gives his own judgment as an apostle who has the Spirit, verse 40. The distinction teaches the church how to listen to Christ: His words are the foundation, and the apostles' words are the application.

It points to Christ by the ground of the whole chapter. 'You were bought at a price,' verse 23, is the line that makes sense of everything before it. The believer, single or married, slave or free, belongs to the one who paid the price. The words of verse 22 are especially pointed: the slave is 'the Lord's freedman' and the free man is 'Christ's slave.' Both statuses are redefined by Christ, and neither gives a person a claim over Him. Paul's gospel is that Christ has become the owner of those who were bound, and in His ownership they are free.

It points to Christ by pattern. The mutual self-giving of verses 3 to 5 is the shape of love that Paul will later find in Christ, who 'loved the church and gave Himself up for her,' Ephesians 5:25. Husbands and wives who yield their bodies to each other, and who do so for the sake of prayer and in the fear of Satan's tempting, are living out a small version of the pattern. And the call to remain where God has put you echoes the Lord's own obedience, since He took the form of a servant, Philippians 2:7, and did not leave the place the Father had given Him until the work was done.

It points to Christ by the picture of marriage. Paul does not mention Christ and the church in this chapter, but the foundation is the same one he will cite in Ephesians 5:31-32, where the one flesh union is said to be about Christ and the church. In a mixed marriage, the believer is the channel by which the holiness of the Lord reaches the household, and the Lord's own household is a mixed one, since even His brothers did not at first believe, John 7:5.

A caution is needed. Paul does not say that a believer's presence saves a spouse; verse 16 asks 'how do you know?' Salvation is Christ's work, and the household is holy because He makes it so.
study.god:
This chapter shows a God who gives gifts and does not demand sameness. 'each man has his own gift from God; one has this gift, another has that,' verse 7. Marriage and singleness are both described as grace, and neither is allowed to boast over the other. The God of the passage is a generous giver whose gifts come in different shapes and who is not threatened by variety in His people. Churches that rank one calling over the other have misunderstood Him.

It shows a God who cares about the ordinary details of human life. The passage speaks about sex, divorce, a difficult spouse, children, a slave's freedom and a man's circumcision. These are not spiritual topics in the narrow sense, and yet Paul treats each as a place where God has an interest and a word. 'The Lord has assigned' the life each person leads, verse 17, and that assignment covers the household, the workshop and the bedroom. The God of the Bible is not remote from the details.

It shows a God of peace. Verse 15 says that 'God has called you to live in peace,' which is the reason a believer is released from an abandoned marriage and the reason the believing spouse should not force the issue. He does not call His people to a life of constant conflict. Where peace can be kept, it should be kept, and where an unbeliever breaks it, the believer is not enslaved to the quarrel.

It shows a God who is holy and who spreads holiness. The idea that an unbelieving spouse and children are 'sanctified' is a statement about God's way. In the Old Testament, holiness and uncleanness were thought of as things that could spread, and the common assumption was that the unclean contaminated the clean. Paul says that in Christ the flow runs the other way, since holiness is stronger than defilement. That is a very high view of what God does through a single believer in a house.

It shows a God who owns. 'You were bought at a price' is a sentence about God's right over His people, and it is stated as a reason for freedom from every human claim. In worship, this leads to thankfulness for the generosity of the gifts, to trust that every station in life can be offered to Him, and to humility about the limits of what we know, since Paul himself says 'how do you know?' in verse 16 and leaves the outcome with God.

crossReferences.note: God sees that it is not good for the man to be alone and brings the woman to him, and the two become one flesh. This is the foundation for everything Paul says about mutual belonging in marriage, and it explains why neither partner can treat the body as a private possession.

Even in a society with a different structure of marriage, the law protects a wife's food, clothing and marital rights. The idea that marriage creates an obligation of this kind is old. Paul's 'marital duty' in verse 3 gives it a fully mutual form.

'I belong to my beloved and he belongs to me.' The mutual belonging that Paul describes in verse 4 has its warmest expression in the Song, which shows that his language of authority over the body is the language of love and not a dry legal formula.

Jesus answers a question about divorce by taking His hearers back to creation and then speaks about both husband and wife divorcing. Paul's 'not I, but the Lord' points to this tradition, and the symmetry of the wording fits the Roman setting in which women could also initiate a divorce.

Jesus gives His teaching on divorce, with the exception for sexual immorality, and then the disciples respond that it is better not to marry. He speaks of those who have been given the gift of singleness. This text lies behind Paul's pairing of the two gifts in verse 7.

The prophet says that the LORD was witness between a man and the wife of his youth and that He hates divorce. It provides the Old Testament background for the Lord's command in verses 10 and 11 and shows that the seriousness of the marriage covenant is not a new teaching.

The returning exiles covenanted to send away their foreign wives and children. Paul's instruction in verses 12 to 14 runs the opposite way for believers married to unbelievers, because holiness is now thought to flow from the believer to the household and not the other way around.

Wives who are married to unbelieving husbands are told that they may win them without words by their reverent behaviour. It makes concrete what Paul means by the hope of verse 16, and it shows that the believing spouse's task is a quiet, patient witness, not pressure.

Paul and Silas tell the jailer that he will be saved, 'you and your household,' and the whole household is baptised and rejoices. The story shows the way the gospel moved through households in Paul's own ministry, and it sheds light on his words about the holiness of the believer's family.

Neither circumcision nor uncircumcision has value in Christ Jesus; what matters is faith expressed through love. This is the same principle as verse 19, put in a positive form. Paul wants people to stop treating status markers as ultimate.

Paul tells Philemon to receive Onesimus 'no longer as a slave, but better than a slave, as a beloved brother.' It shows how the principle of verses 21 and 22 worked in practice. The slave remains in his situation, but the relationship has been changed from within.

Paul quotes Genesis 2:24 and says the mystery is about Christ and the church. It shows the deepest meaning he saw in the one flesh union that lies behind this chapter, and it keeps readers from reducing his teaching on marriage to a list of duties.

study.oneStory:
The Bible opens with a marriage. In Genesis 2, God brings the woman to the man, and the first human words recorded are a song of recognition, 'bone of my bones.' The first command to humanity includes being fruitful, Genesis 1:28, and the first thing God calls not good is solitude. Chapter 7 draws on all of this, and it shows how a good gift is both honoured and relativised in the light of what comes next.

The fall twisted the gift. By Genesis 3:16 the harmony of the couple has become rivalry, and in the story that follows, marriages are broken by polygamy, jealousy and the use of one partner by another. The law of Moses regulated divorce and protected the vulnerable partner, but the Lord's own answer in the Gospels is that that it was not this way from the beginning, Matthew 19:8, and Paul takes up that restored vision. Chapter 7 is the New Testament's practical working-out of what it means to live in a marriage, or outside one, as a person who has been redeemed.

The passage also sets up the end of the story. If marriage is a sign of Christ and the church, then single and married alike are looking forward to the wedding that it points to, Revelation 19:7-9, in which the bride is the whole people of God. The institution gives way to its goal, not because it is bad but because it has done its work, as Jesus said that in the resurrection people 'will neither marry nor be given in marriage,' Luke 20:35. That is part of why Paul can honour singleness without belittling marriage.

Within the story, the call to remain in one's situation shows what it means to live between the ages. The slave is not yet free in law, the married person is not yet beyond the need for marriage, and the circumcised man is not required to hide his history. Each is called to live as Christ's person in the situation he has, trusting that the Lord who bought him will finish what He began. The new creation will not abolish these people and their stories, but it will fulfil them, and in it, those bought at a price will be at home.

quiz.q: What does Paul teach about sexual duty within marriage?

options.text: Husband and wife each belong to the other and should not deprive one another, except briefly by mutual consent.
options.note: Verses 3 to 5 teach mutual self-giving and warn against withholding.

options.text: The husband alone has authority, and the wife must simply submit.
options.note: Paul strikingly makes the authority mutual: each has authority over the other's body.

options.text: Married couples should abstain permanently to be more spiritual.
options.note: Paul warns that prolonged deprivation opens the door to temptation.

options.text: Sexual duty may be set aside indefinitely for prayer.
options.note: Only for a time and by mutual consent; then come together again.

quiz.q: How does Paul regard marriage and singleness?

options.text: Each is a gift from God, suited to different people.
options.note: Verse 7 calls each state a charisma, a gift of grace.

options.text: Singleness is holy and marriage is a lesser compromise.
options.note: Paul honors both; he does not treat marriage as merely inferior.

options.text: Marriage is commanded for everyone.
options.note: Paul commends singleness too and wishes others could share his gift.

options.text: Both are burdens to be endured, not gifts.
options.note: Paul explicitly calls each a gift from God.

quiz.q: What is the Lord's own command to the married?

options.text: A wife must not separate from her husband, and a husband must not divorce his wife.
options.note: Verses 10 to 11 relay Jesus' command against divorce.

options.text: Couples may divorce freely if they are unhappy.
options.note: This is the opposite of the Lord's command.

options.text: A separated wife may remarry anyone at once.
options.note: Paul says she should remain unmarried or be reconciled.

options.text: Only the husband is bound; the wife is free.
options.note: The command binds both husband and wife alike.

quiz.q: What does Paul say about a marriage where only one spouse believes?

options.text: The believer should stay if the unbeliever is willing, for the home is sanctified.
options.note: Verses 12 to 14 urge the believer not to divorce a willing unbelieving spouse.

options.text: The believer must divorce the unbeliever to stay pure.
options.note: Paul says the reverse: do not divorce a willing spouse.

options.text: The believer may leave only if the unbeliever departs.
options.note: True in part; if the unbeliever leaves, let him go, but the believer should not initiate it.

options.text: The marriage is meaningless and should be ignored.
options.note: Paul takes it seriously, saying the home is set apart and the spouse may yet be saved.

quiz.q: What is the governing principle Paul repeats in verses 17 to 24?

options.text: Each believer should remain faithful to God in the situation to which he was called.
options.note: The refrain is to live out the calling in the place God's call found you.

options.text: Every believer must change their circumstances after conversion.
options.note: Paul teaches the opposite: remain in your calling.

options.text: Outward status like circumcision determines your standing with God.
options.note: Paul says circumcision is nothing; keeping God's commandments counts.

options.text: Slaves should never seek freedom under any circumstances.
options.note: Paul does say gain your freedom if you can, though the main point is faithful contentment.

quiz.q: Why can a believer serve God contentedly in any station of life?

options.text: Because they were bought at a price and belong to the Lord.
options.note: Verse 23 grounds identity in Christ's purchase, above every earthly status.

options.text: Because earthly circumstances do not matter at all to God.
options.note: They matter, but they are relativized by belonging to Christ.

options.text: Because status can be earned through hard work.
options.note: The point is redemption received, not status earned.

options.text: Because freedom is the only truly Christian condition.
options.note: Paul values freedom, but says even a slave is the Lord's freedman.

questions: Paul teaches that husband and wife belong to one another in mutual self-giving. If you are married, where might selfishness be creeping in, and what would generous love look like instead?
Both singleness and marriage are called gifts from God. How can you receive your current season, whichever it is, as a genuine gift rather than a lack?
The Lord commands married believers not to divorce. What does it look like to fight for your marriage, or to honor the permanence of marriage in how you speak of it?
A believing spouse can be a means of grace in the home. If you share a home with someone who does not believe, how might your quiet faithfulness point them to Christ?
Remain in the calling in which you were called. Are you waiting for different circumstances to serve God, when He is calling you to be faithful right where you are?

translationNotes.note: It is good to abstain from sexual relations renders a phrase that reads literally not to touch a woman, an idiom for sexual relations; many read it as a Corinthian slogan Paul takes up and carefully qualifies in the verses that follow.

Paul distinguishes the Lord's own command, do not divorce, from his own apostolic instruction to the rest; this marks which words trace directly to Jesus' earthly teaching, not a difference in authority.
Sanctified here means set apart within the sphere of grace and covenant, not automatically saved; verse 16 still asks whether the spouse will be saved, showing personal faith is needed.
Bought at a price echoes 6:20, applying the language of redemption to every station of life; because Christ owns us, no earthly status finally defines us.
